messages.content:
Implement one complete standalone child-facing HTML evaluation from the immutable academic and design artifacts.

Implement the artifacts faithfully. You own implementation details needed to make the declared interaction work, but you may not add another design doctrine, change academic content, expose an answer before the first committed response, or make learning conclusions.

The document must work at the declared viewport with touch and mouse and no keyboard requirement. The child must always be able to continue after an incorrect, uncertain, or instrument-ambiguous response. Every queried DOM element must exist before JavaScript accesses it. Use no parent application endpoints, cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, currency, browser speech synthesis, or oscillator audio.

Post evaluation_ready, evaluation_attempt, evaluation_friction, and evaluation_complete messages to window.parent. Every attempt must include itemId, constructId, result, assistance, exposure, responseMode, possibleConfounds, and attemptedValue. Return one complete HTML document and nothing else.

TARGET VIEWPORT
1365×768

{
  "artifactId": "juniper:eval-design:LAB-MATH-GEOMETRY-FACES-5-11:opening:v1:museum-of-mystery-solids",
  "upstreamHash": "357e7ae9a9243586a072d9bb454180bf3f7fb63793f6cec1128c39b2781cffb0",
  "title": "The Museum of Mystery Solids: Night Curator",
  "designRationale": "Reina is nine, has shown appetite for hard problems, notices logical inconsistencies, and responded well to clear examples and visible color. That evidence tells me two things I commit to: (1) she will tolerate a five-item sequence without candy-coated rewards if the fiction respects her intelligence, and (2) she will detect and resent fake feedback, so the design must be honest that no verdicts arrive until the end. I chose a 'night curator in a museum of solids' frame because a curator's job — examining objects and filing accurate records — makes withholding correctness feel natural and dignified rather than withheld: museum records are sealed until the ledger closes. That solves the hardest constraint (zero feedback, zero hints, zero teaching before commitment) narratively instead of mechanically. Every item is a pedestal exhibit; the child's job is to complete the exhibit's record card by selecting from fixed plaque options. Rotatable 3D-rendered solids (drag to orbit) directly serve C4: a child who can rotate the pyramid can discover the hidden square base by her own action, which is legitimate observation, not teaching — the contract measures reasoning about face composition, not memory of hidden faces, and orbiting is available identically on every item so it adds no differential exposure. The single permitted non-teaching clarification is embodied as a 'Reread the task' plaque button that only restates navigation/format ('Pick one card' / 'Pick every card that is true'), logged as hintRequested. The design deliberately refuses a score screen, stars, or mastery language; the payoff is the ledger closing and the museum lights coming on, reporting only factual completion.",
  "independentlyChosenPrinciples": [
    "Honesty before charm: no interface element may imply correctness or incorrectness before the evaluation ends, and the fiction must make that silence feel purposeful, not withholding.",
    "The child's hands should touch the mathematics: rotating the actual solid is the core physical act, so the evidence reflects 3D reasoning rather than picture-decoding skill.",
    "Commitment is sacred: a response is only recorded when the child stamps the record card; everything before the stamp (selection, deselection, rotation) is exploration and is logged as option-change telemetry, never punished.",
    "No trap states: skip is always visible, always neutral in tone, and never framed as failure ('Leave this exhibit for the day curator').",
    "Reading is not the construct: prompts stay under 25 words, options are short cards with both a word and a small plane-figure glyph where the contract's options are shape names, and nothing requires typing.",
    "Respect the observer: every logged key is factual (what was selected, when, after how many changes), and the closing report states attempts, assistance, exposure, friction, and completion — never mastery.",
    "Color carries meaning only for attention, never for correctness: the highlighted face in I2 uses a single accent hue reserved exclusively for 'the surface being asked about'."
  ],
  "openingPromise": "\"The museum is dark. Five mystery solids arrived tonight, and their record cards are blank. You are the Night Curator — examine each one and file its true record before morning.\" One sentence, spoken and shown, over a dim gallery with five glowing pedestals.",
  "firstThreeSeconds": "Second 0–1: dim museum gallery fades in, five pedestals in a row, the nearest spotlit; a rotating cylinder/sphere/prism/cone quartet gleams on it. Second 1–2: a clipboard slides up from the bottom edge with the I1 prompt and four large option cards. Second 2–3: a soft pulsing halo on the nearest solid plus a one-line cue: \"Drag a solid to turn it. Tap a card to answer.\" Nothing else moves; the required action is the only lit, pulsing thing on screen.",
  "firstAction": "Drag any of the four spotlit I1 solids to rotate it (optional exploration), then tap one of the four large option cards on the clipboard and press the big STAMP button to file the record. The stamp button is disabled-dim until a card is selected, so the causal chain (choose, then commit) is visible before any touch happens.",
  "mission": "Restore the Museum of Mystery Solids before the morning bell: five exhibits, five blank record cards. Each correctly examined-and-filed record card (filed, not judged — filing is completion, not correctness) advances the night clock and lights another wing of the museum. When the fifth card is stamped or set aside, the ledger seals, the lights come on, and the Night Curator's shift report is issued.",
  "coreInteraction": "Per exhibit: (1) read a short plaque prompt (≤25 words, also read aloud via a tap-to-listen speaker icon so reading is never the gate); (2) freely drag-rotate the pictured solid(s) in real 3D with momentum and snap-back, on touch or mouse; (3) tap option cards on the record clipboard — single-select items swap the selection, multi-select items toggle cards with a visible 'selected' pin, and I5's 'none of them' card auto-unpins all others with a visible animation so the exclusivity rule is shown, not read; (4) press STAMP to commit. The stamp is one large 96px target. After stamping, the pedestal's record slot fills with a wax-sealed card (contents hidden), the exhibit light dims to 'archived amber', and the walkway to the next pedestal illuminates. A 'Reread the task' button restates only the response format and navigation; it is logged as hintRequested and teaches nothing about flatness, faces, or shapes.",
  "mathAsPower": "The mathematics IS the curator's instrument: the only way to fill a record card truthfully is to reason about the solid's actual surfaces. Rotation makes face-set reasoning physically powerful — turning the square pyramid reveals the base a silhouette hides (C4), and turning the sphere shows there is nowhere flat to rest a card (C1/C3). The child's geometric judgment is what moves the night forward: each stamped record lights a wing of the museum, and no other action in the world does anything. There is no combat proxy, no timer proxy; discriminating flat from curved and naming face shapes is the sole lever of progress.",
  "responseAffordances": "All responses are large tap targets: option cards minimum 220×110px with generous spacing at 1365×768, stamp button 96px circular, skip link a full-width quiet bar. Single-select: tapping a card selects it and visibly deselects the previous one (swap animation), so changing one's mind is one tap. Multi-select: cards toggle with a pin/unpin animation; at least one pin required before STAMP enables (matching I3's rule); I5's exclusivity rule for 'none of them' is enforced by visible auto-unpinning. Every option card for shape-name options (I2, and the set descriptions in I4) carries a small monochrome plane-figure glyph beside the word so the answer does not depend on reading the word 'rectangle' — the glyph is a flat 2D icon, never a picture of the solid, so it cannot leak the answer. Tap-to-listen narration on every prompt and every option card. No typing, no dragging-to-precise-targets, no double-tap, no long-press, no keyboard. Rotation uses forgiving full-object hit areas. optionChangeCount is logged from card toggles before the stamp.",
  "stakesAndConsequences": "Stakes are diegetic and dignified: an unfiled record means a dark wing of the museum, and the morning bell fiction gives urgency without any actual timer (timeLimit is 'none' per contract; the clock advances only on stamps/skips, never on real time). Consequences of stamping are real and irreversible within the night — a stamped card is wax-sealed and cannot be reopened, which makes commitment meaningful and protects evidence independence. A skipped exhibit gets a visibly different 'day curator' tag, honestly recorded as noResponse. Nothing in the world ever labels a stamped card right or wrong; the stakes are about completing the shift truthfully, which is exactly what the instrument needs the child to believe.",
  "recovery": "No response can trap the child. Before stamping, any selection can be changed freely with single taps and is logged only as optionChangeCount. If the child stamps with an answer she is unsure of, the world reacts identically to any stamp — seal, amber light, walkway forward — so uncertainty is never exposed or punished. If she stalls, after 45 seconds of no input a gentle non-teaching nudge appears once per item: \"Take your time. You can turn the solid, pick a card, or leave this one for the day curator.\" (navigation-only; logged as idleNudgeShown, distinct from hintRequested). Skip is always one tap and moves her forward with the same walkway animation. Accidental taps cannot commit anything because only STAMP commits. Early exit is available from a persistent quiet door icon: exiting mid-shift seals the ledger with reached items recorded and unreached items marked notAdministered, and the exit screen thanks the curator for the records filed — no failure framing.",
  "progression": "Fixed order I1→I5, presented as five pedestals along one gallery corridor, so progress is spatially legible: the child can always see how many exhibits remain by looking down the hall. A night-clock at the top advances one hour per terminal item (stamped or skipped), from 1am to 6am. Each completed exhibit lights its wing with a distinct architectural silhouette (rotunda, arch hall, glass atrium, stairwell, dome), giving a visible, non-evaluative progression reward. No difficulty is announced; the pedestals simply differ in what they hold, matching the contract's fixed item order and boundaries exactly.",
  "worldReaction": "Correct, incorrect, and uncertain stamps all produce the same truthful reaction: the wax seal presses down with a satisfying thunk, the card slides into the pedestal drawer, the exhibit dims to archived amber, the clock ticks one hour, and the next walkway lights. Changed selections before stamping produce a soft card-swap sound and pin animations — acknowledgment without judgment. A skip produces a gentler reaction: the card is clipped to the pedestal with a 'for the day curator' tag, same clock tick, same walkway. The rotation of solids gives continuous physical feedback (inertia, subtle specular highlights moving across flat faces as planes and across curved surfaces as sweeping bands — a truthful physical property of the render, present on every solid equally, not an added answer cue). Nothing ever glows green, buzzes red, or replays the item. Answer exposure is structurally impossible: sealed cards show only a seal.",
